newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Wessex yr profits up, eyes spend.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Wessex yr profits up, eyes spend.

text.p: British water and sewerage company Wessex Water Plc is expected to turn in higher profits and dividend when it reports annual results on June 25, but low gearing will be the key issue, analysts said.
"It's one of the lowest-geared companies in the sector and we'll be looking to see what the strategy is," said one analyst who asked not to be identified.
Wessex should pump up annual pretax profits to 144.4-147.4 million stg from 133.9 million a year ago and pay out a total dividend of 17.2-17.8 pence per share compared with 15.2 previously.
Wessex was blocked by the government from plans to make a bid for fellow water firm South West Water in October 1996 along with rival Severn Trent Water.
The company then made a package of share buybacks and bought back most of the 19.5 percent stake in it held by Waste Management International.
"It's unlikely Wessex will want to do any more capital restructuring before the budget," the analyst said.

The new Labour government has vowed to introduce a one-off tax on the "excess profits" of privatised utilities at its first budget on July 2 and companies are expected to keep shareholder benefits muted until then.
Water companies are also under fire for their handling of the country's current drought, the worst in 200 years, and are facing mandatory targets to cut leakage.

Analysts said Wessex might be more likely to consider spending on an acquisition and added that a likely target was taking full control of UK Waste, its joint venture with Waste Management International.
"The most logical deal for Wessex would be to buy the remaining 50 percent. But it's not clear it would be up for sale," the analyst said.
Estimates put the cost of such an acquisition at around 150 million stg which would still only bring Wessex's gearing to sector averages.
"Whatever they decide they can do, we are at least expecting a strategy statement from them," the analyst said.
"Cost cut benefits are slowing and they need to find something to sustain dividend growth," he added. -- Jo Winterbottom, London Newsroom +44171 542 7717
